name: Kira Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for talking to me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no links to AI companies, employers or government. What you say is confidential. Could you describe a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Greenleaf Grill, the chain family restaurant in the town centre, on cold starters and desserts. I do salads, the prawn cocktails, and about sixty brownies and cheesecakes a day, all from the chain's spec cards. I'm junior, so the sous chef checks my plating against the photo. I like desserts because they're calm compared to the grill.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do things look outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a flat with a friend from school, Jade, near the bus station. I've got about two weeks' rent saved, never more. Greenleaf shut two of its branches in other towns last year, which made everyone twitchy. I use AI now and then, mostly to sort my budget or reword a message to the landlord.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a tool, like the calculator. At work I'd say the real thing to watch is whether people keep eating out. I'm not very political online, I'd probably just share a funny meme about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my worry stays the same: the chain shutting branches. If people are tight with money, they skip the family meal out, and then head office looks at our numbers. AI flopping doesn't change that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my section well so I'm not first on the list. I'd start doing birthday cakes for friends of friends on Saturdays, maybe two a month at forty each. And I'd keep my phone contract and the gym, nothing fancy to cut anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Twitchy, same as now. It's like hearing a car alarm down the street every night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did it feel like when the other two branches closed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We heard on a Tuesday through a group chat, before head office said anything. A girl I'd trained with at the other branch got two weeks' notice. She's on a supermarket bakery counter now, earning less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why birthday cakes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because desserts are the one thing I'm actually decent at. My cheesecakes get compliments, and the cake decorating I picked up from videos. Two cakes a month would be a phone bill paid.

say: I'd say AI is a **tool, like a calculator**.
I'd say the real thing to watch is **eating out** spending.
think: My worry stays the **chain shutting branches**.
Tight customers skip the family meal, then **head office** looks at our numbers.
do: Keep my **section sharp** so I'm not first on the cut list.
Make **two birthday cakes** a month at forty each on Saturdays.
feel: **Twitchy**, like a car alarm down the street every night.
S0.quote: We heard on a Tuesday through a group chat, before head office said anything.
fieldNote: Kira's fear is **chain closures**, which AI Plateau does nothing to ease.
She watched a **trainee friend** get two weeks' notice and take a lower-paid job.
Desserts are her **one strength**, so she builds a side income there.

steps.text: Keep the cold starters and desserts section spotless at Greenleaf Grill
Bake two birthday cakes a month for friends of friends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it makes sense, if it's done fairly. At work I'd say let's see what head office does with it. Online I'd keep quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully? Chains move first, and head office already plans our menus and orders centrally. AI would make that even tighter, and maybe they'd decide one fewer cook on the desserts is fine. I'm hands-on, but I'm also the junior.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn whatever app head office sends down quickly, once I see the sous chef using it. I'd try to save thirty a week from the cake money. If the chain started trialling dessert machines, I'd start looking at independent places straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm not dramatic about it, but I'd notice every email from head office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which apps do you think head office would send?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably something for waste and stock, telling us exactly how many cheesecakes to defrost. We already have a tablet for temperature checks. If it's like that, I'd pick it up fine after a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look at independent places. Are there any nearby?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two, really. A bakery café on the market square and an Italian place that only hires family. Not many choices, which is the whole problem with this town.

fieldNote: Kira sees **chain ownership** as her biggest exposure to automation.

steps.text: Learn the head office stock and waste app within a week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow down, nobody voted for this. At work I'd say look after each other. Online I might share something asking what the plan is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, chains will want robots the minute they're ready, around 2031, because they make the same cheesecake two thousand times. Before that, AI runs head office and they'll close more branches to save money. I think I lose the Greenleaf job within three or four years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move to the bakery café on the market square in the first year if they'd have me, even for less, because small places change slower. I'd push the cakes harder, aiming for one a week. I'd cut the gym and stop eating out with Jade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Properly worried. Like I've been told to leave a party but I don't have a lift home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would a small bakery change slower?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The old woman who owns the bakery café is about seventy and still writes orders on a pad. She'll never buy a robot. She doesn't even have a card machine that works. That's not a great business plan, but it's a slower one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the flat with Jade if your pay drops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably need a third flatmate, which means me moving into the box room. Jade works in a call centre, so her job might be worse than mine. We've joked about both moving back home.

I'd tell the team to **look after each other**.
I might share a post online asking **what the plan** is.

I expect to **lose the Greenleaf job** within three or four years.

Her **flatmate's call centre** job makes the household more fragile.

steps.text: Apply to the market square bakery café in the first year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough warning, so let's use it. At work I'd say think about what you'd do next. Online I'd stay out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, eight years till robots do desserts, and probably less at a chain. That's enough for me to get a qualification. I'm not the quickest learner, but I'm stubborn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a year to see which way the chains go. Then I'd do the evening pastry certificate at the college, one night a week for two years. I'd keep Greenleaf as long as they keep me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but okay. More like exam nerves than panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the certificate get you that you don't have now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A proper pastry job, maybe at a hotel or a wedding cake business, where it's more handmade. And I left school early, so the pastry certificate would be the first certificate I've got. My mum would put it on the fridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait a year first. What if that year costs you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have lost a year. But I've seen people jump into courses and the jobs weren't there. I'd rather watch for a bit, that's just how I am.

I'd tell coworkers to **think about what's next**.
I'd **stay out of it** online, as usual.
think: I'd have **eight years** till robots do desserts, maybe less at a chain.
I'm **stubborn**, even if I'm not the quickest learner.
do: Wait **one year** to see which way the chains go.
Do the evening **pastry certificate** one night a week for two years.

S3.quote: I left school early, so the pastry certificate would be the first certificate I've got. My mum would put it on the fridge.
fieldNote: Kira wants a **first qualification** as much for pride as for work.
Her one-year **wait** shows a steady person who likes proof first.
She still expects the **chain job to go**, which keeps her anxious.

steps.text: Watch for a year how chains bring in kitchen robots

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so no excuses for anyone. At work I'd say start a plan now. I'd still keep my head down online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thirteen years to the robots means I'd be forty, and by then I'd want to be good at something specific. Wedding cakes, maybe, the handmade fancy ones people pay for. But the chain could still close my branch next year, AI or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the pastry certificate in the first year or two, once a friend's done it and said it's worth it. I'd build the cake orders into a small business with a proper hygiene rating from the council. I'd try to have two months' rent saved by the time I'm thirty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steadier. Still the old worry about the chain, but less of a deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wedding cakes in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because people want a person for those, someone who listens to the bride's ideas and gets it right. A robot can do sixty cheesecakes, but I don't think anyone wants a robot at the cake tasting. And they pay four or five hundred.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to get there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A cake fridge and a bigger oven, maybe eight hundred together. And a kitchen that passes inspection, which my flat doesn't. I'd look for a shared kitchen to rent by the hour.

I'd keep my **head down online**, same as always.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the chain would cut me fast and there's hardly anywhere else to go in this town. What would help is cheap evening courses and a small grant to start a home business properly. Maybe a rule that chains have to give more notice when they close.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask about towns like mine. There's two kitchens to choose from in my town if the chain restaurant I work at goes. People in cities can just walk down the road for a new job.

headlineQuote: There's two kitchens to choose from in my town if the chain restaurant I work at goes.
portrait: Kira is a 27-year-old **junior dessert cook** at a chain family restaurant in a small town.
She shares a flat, has **two weeks' rent** saved, and fears branch closures.
She is pragmatic and steady, learning new tools **once colleagues have**.
She sees **handmade cakes** as her way to stay ahead of robots.
Her mood stays **anxious** throughout, rising to alarmed under fast AGI.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with the chain cutting fast and almost nowhere else to go.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap evening courses** and a small grant for a home business.
